questions.question: Are there climatetech-specific grants or public funding programs available in Berlin or Brandenburg?

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: Key programs: Exist Gründerstipendium (if you have university affiliation), ILB ProBrand in Brandenburg (up to €200k for innovative Brandenburg-based startups), and the European Innovation Council (EIC) Accelerator for deep climate tech. Also check BMWK funding calls — several are climate-specific.

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: From a tax angle: R&D tax credits (Forschungslagengesetz) are underused by Berlin startups. If your climate tech involves genuine R&D, you can claim 25% of R&D personnel costs back as a tax credit — up to €1M per year. Your Steuerberater must apply for this explicitly.

answers.name: Hana Okafor
answers.text: We combined Exist with a KfW Energy Efficiency grant for our hardware component. Stacking non-dilutive funding from multiple programs is legal and common — just make sure the use-of-funds do not overlap between applications.

questions.question: Which Berlin coworking spaces have a strong sustainability or climatetech community?

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: EUREF Campus in Schöneberg is the best in Berlin for climatetech — it is a dedicated energy and mobility hub with Vattenfall, startups, and research institutions on site. The Delta in Mitte is strong for general tech and has a growing sustainability cluster. Both are worth a visit before committing.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: We tried three spaces before settling. The Delta won us over because the community is curated — they are selective about who joins, which means the quality of spontaneous conversations is high. For a climatetech team, the cross-pollination with other impact startups there is real.

answers.name: Sofia Almeida
answers.text: Also look at Supermarkt Berlin in Wedding — it is a cooperative coworking space with a strong sustainability ethos and a community of freelancers, NGOs, and impact startups. Cheaper than The Delta and EUREF, good if budget is tight at pre-seed.

questions.question: Which Berlin VCs are actively investing in climatetech pre-seed rounds right now?

answers.name: Priya Nandakumar
answers.text: Active Berlin-based climatetech investors at pre-seed: Vireo Ventures (dedicated climate fund), UVC Partners (deep tech including climate), and World Fund (Europe-wide but Berlin-headquartered, very active). Also look at Ecosummit Berlin — it is the best climatetech investor event in the city.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: Do not overlook corporate VCs: BASF Ventures, Vattenfall Ventures, and Bosch Ventures all have Berlin presence and write climate-relevant checks. Corporate VCs move slower but can bring pilot customers, which matters more than capital at pre-seed.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: The Ecosummit conference in Berlin is where the serious climatetech investors show up. Apply to pitch there — even if you do not win, the hallway conversations with World Fund and Vireo are worth the trip.

questions.question: How do I build an investor pitch deck for a deeptech pre-seed round?

answers.name: Jonas Reuter
answers.text: Deeptech decks need one extra slide non-deeptech decks do not: a credibility slide. Show your teams technical background, any IP, publications, or patents. Investors need to believe you can build what you are describing before they care about the market. Keep it to 12 slides max.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: The biggest mistake deeptech founders make is spending 8 slides on technology and 2 on business model. Flip it. Investors fund businesses, not research projects. Lead with the problem and market, then explain why your tech is the unfair advantage.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: Get a demo in front of investors as early as possible — even a rough prototype. Deeptech is hard to evaluate from slides alone. A working demo, even limited, builds confidence faster than any deck.

questions.question: How do I find product-market fit as a B2B deeptech startup with a long sales cycle?

answers.name: Sofia Almeida
answers.text: With long sales cycles, traditional PMF signals (retention, NPS) take too long to arrive. Instead, track leading indicators: do prospects urgently make time to see you? Do they introduce you to colleagues unprompted? Are they willing to pay even for a pilot? These signal real pull before revenue arrives.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: Run paid pilots, not free ones. Paying customers give honest feedback; free users are polite. Even €5k for a 3-month pilot validates willingness to pay and focuses the customer on outcomes.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: Talk to 50 potential customers before you have a product. Map their current workflow in detail. PMF in deeptech is often about inserting yourself into an existing process rather than creating a new one.

questions.question: What does a shareholder agreement need to cover for a two-founder GmbH?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Essential clauses: vesting schedule with cliff, drag-along and tag-along rights, right of first refusal on share transfers, deadlock resolution mechanism, IP assignment (all work done for the company belongs to the company), and good/bad leaver provisions. Do not skip the deadlock clause — it is the one founders regret missing most.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: We skipped the deadlock resolution clause and spent six months in a standoff with no legal mechanism to resolve it. Cost us time, money, and almost the company. Do not skip it.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Also add a non-compete and non-solicitation clause. It feels unnecessary on day one but matters enormously if a co-founder leaves and starts a competing company six months later.

questions.question: What is the Berlin startup networking scene like and where should I show up as a new founder?

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: The Berlin scene is dense and surprisingly accessible. Key recurring events: Founders & Friends (monthly, 300+ people), Tech Open Air satellite events, and various vertical Stammtisch meetups. Show up consistently — Berlin rewards persistence over one-off appearances.

answers.name: Sofia Almeida
answers.text: Do not go to networking events to pitch. Go to learn and help others. Berlin founders have a strong pay-it-forward culture — if you are generous with your knowledge and connections first, the right people will find you.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: Factory Berlin, Mindspace, and the Startup Night Berlin events are the highest-density founder gatherings. LinkedIn is surprisingly active in the Berlin scene too — post thoughtfully and people will reach out.

questions.question: Is Factory Berlin or The Delta better for a Seed-stage edtech team of 6 people?

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: For a team of 6, The Delta is the better fit. Factory Berlin is great for networking but the office products for small teams are expensive and the space feels corporate at that size. The Delta offers dedicated team rooms, a curated community, and better value per desk for 4–8 person teams.

answers.name: Hana Okafor
answers.text: We moved to The Delta after 6 months at a shared space and the productivity jump was immediate. Having a dedicated room your team owns changes the dynamic completely. The Delta also runs regular community events that surface useful connections without you having to go out of your way.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: Do a trial week at both before deciding — both offer this. The vibe difference is real. Factory is buzzy and social; The Delta is more focused and operational. For a Seed team that needs to ship, The Delta wins.

questions.question: We are a Polish-German founding team. Can we structure the GmbH with one founder registered in Poland?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Yes, a non-German EU citizen can be a GmbH shareholder and Geschäftsführer without restriction — EU freedom of establishment applies. Your Polish co-founder does not need to be registered in Germany as long as the GmbH itself has a German registered address. They will need a German tax ID (Steuer-ID) for the notary appointment.

answers.name: Yara Demir
answers.text: EU co-founders have it much easier than non-EU. The main practical issue is the notary appointment — your Polish co-founder needs to be physically present in Berlin or grant a notarised power of attorney (Vollmacht) to someone who can attend in their place.

answers.name: Tomas Berg
answers.text: We had a similar situation with a Swedish co-founder. The Vollmacht route worked fine — your German co-founder can hold the power of attorney. Just make sure the Vollmacht is notarised in Poland with an Apostille, otherwise the Berlin notary will not accept it.

questions.question: We need a part-time CFO or finance advisor for our Seed round preparation. How do founders in Berlin typically find fractional finance help?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: I used a fractional CFO for our Series A prep and it was one of the best investments we made. Find someone who has been through a German VC round specifically — the data room requirements and investor reporting standards in Germany differ from US or UK norms.

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: Several Berlin-based fractional CFOs specifically serve pre-Seed and Seed startups: look at CFO Connect Berlin community and the Interim CFO listings on Heidrick & Struggles and Kienbaum. Budget €2,000–4,000 per month for a serious fractional CFO with VC round experience.

answers.name: Yara Demir
answers.text: Also ask your Steuerberater if they offer CFO-as-a-service — some Berlin startup-focused firms do. It is cheaper and they already know your books, which saves significant onboarding time.

questions.question: What are the best Berlin edtech communities or Stammtisch events for founders?

answers.name: Yara Demir
answers.text: Join the Berlin EdTech WhatsApp group — ask in the EdTech Berlin Meetup for access. It is where the real conversations happen between events. More useful than any formal networking event for finding co-founders, pilots, and warm intros.

answers.name: Jonas Reuter
answers.text: EdTech Berlin Meetup runs quarterly and is the most focused gathering for the sector. Also check out Startup Edu Berlin on Meetup.com and the Digital Learning Lab events run by the Berlin Senat — they bring together founders, teachers, and policy people in the same room.

answers.name: Hana Okafor
answers.text: The healthtech and edtech communities overlap more than you would expect in Berlin — many founders move between both. Attending Female Founders events and Founders & Friends will get you in front of the right people even if the agenda is not edtech-specific.

questions.question: How do I handle VAT as a SaaS company selling to both German and EU customers?

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: For B2B SaaS: sales to German businesses are subject to 19% VAT. Sales to EU businesses with a valid VAT ID are zero-rated under the reverse charge mechanism. Sales to non-EU customers are generally outside scope. Register for the OSS (One Stop Shop) scheme if you sell to EU consumers.

answers.name: Tomas Berg
answers.text: This tripped us up early. Get your VAT ID (Umsatzsteuer-ID) immediately after GmbH formation — it takes 4–6 weeks and you cannot invoice EU customers correctly without it.

answers.name: Hana Okafor
answers.text: Your invoicing software matters here. We use Lexoffice which handles EU VAT rules automatically. Whatever you use, make sure it can generate correct VAT reports for your Steuerberater.

questions.question: We are raising a pre-seed round. Should we use a SAFE note or a convertible loan in Germany?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: In Germany, SAFEs are not yet as standardised as in the US. Most German investors prefer a Wandeldarlehen (convertible loan) as it fits better within GmbH law. That said, some Berlin angels now accept SAFEs — ask your specific investor which they prefer before spending money on legal docs.

answers.name: Priya Nandakumar
answers.text: We used a convertible loan at pre-seed and it worked fine. Key terms to negotiate: valuation cap, discount rate (20% is standard), and maturity date. Keep it simple — a 4-page convertible loan is better than a 20-page one.

answers.name: Yara Demir
answers.text: I raised on a convertible loan as a newcomer founder. One practical tip: make sure the maturity date gives you enough runway to close your next round — 18 months minimum. Anything shorter creates pressure at the worst time.

questions.question: What are the best angel investors in Berlin for fintech startups?

answers.name: Tomas Berg
answers.text: I can intro you to two Berlin fintech angels who are actively writing €25–50k checks. DM me. More broadly, the Berlin Fintech Stammtisch meetup is a great place to get warm intros organically.

answers.name: Priya Nandakumar
answers.text: Look at the FinLeap and Fintech Forum networks — many active angels come from there. Also check APX (Axel Springer + Porsche accelerator) and Cavalry Ventures for fintech pre-seed. LinkedIn is your friend — search for Berlin fintech operators who have had exits.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Do not underestimate operator angels — people who have built and sold fintech companies are often better than financial investors at pre-seed. They bring customers and intros, not just capital.

questions.question: What should a cap table look like after a pre-seed round with two angels?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: A healthy pre-seed cap table with two angels: founders retain 80–85%, angels take 10–15%, leave 5–10% for a future ESOP pool. If angels are taking more than 20% at pre-seed, that is too much dilution before product-market fit.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Model it in a spreadsheet before you close — simulate what Series A dilution looks like from your current cap table. Founders who end up below 40% at Series A struggle to raise Series B. Work backwards from there.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: Use Ledgy or Carta to manage it from day one. Do not manage a cap table in a spreadsheet once you have external investors — errors are costly and hard to fix later.

questions.question: We are applying to Startup Nation Central and need a Berlin-side reference. How do we find the right intro?

answers.name: Priya Nandakumar
answers.text: The Israeli-German startup corridor is active in Berlin — the Israeli Embassy economic attaché is a good first contact. Also reach out to the German-Israeli Chamber of Commerce (AHK Israel) in Berlin, they facilitate exactly these kinds of introductions and move faster than going through Startup Nation Central directly.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: LinkedIn is your best tool here. Search for Berlin-based founders or investors who have previously gone through Startup Nation Central programs — they are almost always willing to give a reference call. The community is tight and pay-it-forward oriented.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: The German Accelerator has a Berlin office and strong Israeli connections. They run a specific German-Israeli track and can provide the reference you need while also opening doors on the Israeli investor side.

questions.question: We are hiring our first two employees and want to offer virtual shares (VSOPs). Which Berlin law firm handles this well?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: For VSOP documentation in Berlin: Orrick, Taylor Wessing, and SMP (Startup-Minded Professionals) all have strong track records with GmbH virtual share programs. SMP is particularly founder-friendly on pricing and has a standardised VSOP template used by many Berlin startups.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: We used SMP for our VSOP setup. Straightforward process, clear documentation, and they have a template that most Berlin investors and future acquirers will recognise. Do not try to DIY a VSOP — the tax and legal interaction is complex enough that lawyer fees are genuinely worth it.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Make sure your VSOP plan includes a good leaver / bad leaver distinction and a change-of-control clause. These are the two provisions that matter most when something actually happens — acquisition or departure. Many startup VSOP templates are weak on both.

questions.question: What Berlin investor events are worth attending in the second half of the year for a future-of-work B2B startup?

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: The best investor conversations in Berlin happen at small dinners, not big conferences. Ask your warm contacts to host or invite you to one — 12-person founder-investor dinners in Mitte or Prenzlauer Berg are where real relationships get built.

answers.name: Priya Nandakumar
answers.text: For H2 in Berlin: Bits & Pretzels (Munich but all Berlin VCs attend), Startup Night Berlin (October, 1,500+ people), and the EarlyBird VC annual gathering if you can get an invite. Also watch for the Berlin Demo Day run by Axel Springer Plug and Play in Q4.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: Tech Open Air (TOA) satellite events in the second half of the year are underrated for investor access — cheaper to attend than the main festival and the crowds are smaller. The side events around TOA week are where the real Berlin VC community shows up.

questions.question: What does a typical ESOP pool look like for a Berlin GmbH at pre-seed and how is it structured legally?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Standard pre-seed ESOP pool for a Berlin GmbH: 10% of shares reserved as virtual options (VSOPs), not real shares. Real share-based ESOPs in a GmbH are expensive to administer due to notary requirements for every transfer. VSOPs are economically equivalent and far more practical — they are contractual rights, not actual GmbH shares.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: From a tax perspective: VSOPs are taxed as income at exercise (not grant), which is straightforward for employees. Real shares in a GmbH trigger a dry income problem — employees owe tax before they can sell. VSOPs avoid this entirely and are the Berlin startup standard.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: We used a 10% VSOP pool at pre-seed, expanded to 15% before Series A. Investors will expect to see the pool already created before they invest — do not leave it as a post-money discussion, it will cost you more dilution.

questions.question: How do we find our first B2C customers in Berlin without a marketing budget?

answers.name: Sofia Almeida
answers.text: Berlin is a great test market. Start with your immediate network, then expand via Facebook Groups, Reddit communities, and local Meetup groups relevant to your problem space. Offer free or heavily discounted early access in exchange for feedback and referrals.

answers.name: Hana Okafor
answers.text: We posted in Berlin expat Facebook groups and got our first 50 users that way. Also try local community boards (Kiez-level), university notice boards, and Instagram with Berlin-specific hashtags. Do things that do not scale at first.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: Talk to 20 potential customers before building anything else. Berlin has a culture of directness — people will give you honest feedback if you approach them genuinely. Offer a coffee, not a sales pitch.

questions.question: I am on a non-EU visa. Can I be a GmbH co-founder and geschäftsführer at the same time?

answers.name: Yara Demir
answers.text: I went through this exact process. Key tip: have your business plan, proof of funding, and GmbH formation documents ready before your Ausländerbehörde appointment. They will ask for all of it. The Make it in Germany website has a good checklist.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Yes, you can be both shareholder and Geschäftsführer of a GmbH on a non-EU visa, but you will need to apply for a Niederlassungserlaubnis or a specific founder visa (Aufenthaltserlaubnis zur Ausübung einer selbständigen Tätigkeit). The Ausländerbehörde Berlin has a dedicated startup unit — book early, wait times are long.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Also talk to a Rechtsanwalt specialising in immigration before your appointment — not just a startup lawyer. The visa question and the GmbH question are separate legal domains and you need someone who understands both.

questions.question: What Berlin accelerators are worth applying to for a healthtech pre-seed startup?

answers.name: Hana Okafor
answers.text: We went through Flying Health. The clinical network access was the main value — they got us into 3 pilot hospitals in 6 months. The equity they take (typically 5–8%) is worth it at pre-seed if you need those connections.

answers.name: Priya Nandakumar
answers.text: For healthtech pre-seed: Flying Health (Berlin-based, healthtech specialist), Charité BIH Accelerator (academic/clinical connections), and APX for general pre-seed with a strong Berlin network. Flying Health is the most sector-relevant.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Also look at grants before accelerators — Exist Gründerstipendium and Invest (BAFA) are non-dilutive and substantial. Many healthtech founders leave this money on the table by going straight to equity funding.

questions.question: What grants are available for healthtech startups in Berlin?

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: Key ones: Exist Gründerstipendium (up to €150k, non-dilutive, needs university connection), Invest (BAFA, 20% cashback on angel investments), and ProFIT Berlin (IBB, up to €500k for innovative Berlin startups). Apply for Exist first if you have any university affiliation.

answers.name: Hana Okafor
answers.text: We got Exist and it funded our first year. The application is time-consuming but worth it. The key is framing your innovation clearly — the jury wants to see defensible technology, not just a better UX.

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: From a tax perspective: grants are taxable income in Germany but you can offset them against R&D expenses. Make sure your Steuerberater tracks grant income separately from the start.

questions.question: How do I vet a technical co-founder before giving away equity?

answers.name: Jonas Reuter
answers.text: Run a paid trial project together for 4–6 weeks before discussing equity. Evaluate: code quality, communication under pressure, how they handle disagreement, and whether they can ship independently. References from past colleagues are more valuable than any interview.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: The trial project is the only real filter. Also assess culture fit — you will spend more time with this person than with anyone else. Technical skills can be tested; values and work ethic are harder to fake over 6 weeks.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: Talk to people they have worked with before — not references they give you, but people you find yourself via LinkedIn. Ask specifically: would you work with this person again? The answer tells you everything.

questions.question: We need to hire our first engineer. Should we hire a contractor or a full-time employee in Germany?

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: In Germany, the risk of Scheinselbständigkeit (false self-employment) is real — if a contractor works exclusively for you, on your equipment, following your hours, the Finanzamt can reclassify them as an employee and back-charge all social contributions. For a core early engineer, full-time employment is cleaner and signals commitment.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: We hired contractors first and had to convert two of them later — painful and expensive. If you want someone for more than 6 months and they are working primarily for you, just hire them. The legal risk of misclassification in Germany is not worth it.

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: If you do go the contractor route short-term, have your Steuerberater review the contract. Multiple clients, own equipment, and flexible hours are the key factors that support genuine self-employment status.

questions.question: What is a fair equity split between two co-founders at pre-seed?

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: The split matters less than the vesting terms and the co-founder agreement. I have seen 50/50 partnerships fail because there was no buyout mechanism and 60/40 partnerships thrive because everything was documented. Get the agreement done before you need it.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: 50/50 is the simplest and often the best for equal co-founders — it signals trust and avoids resentment. If contributions are unequal, use a vesting schedule (4 years, 1-year cliff) to protect both parties rather than an unequal split. Never start without a vesting agreement.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Investors prefer equal or near-equal splits at pre-seed — big imbalances (e.g. 70/30) raise questions about co-founder alignment. If you go unequal, be ready to explain your reasoning clearly in every investor conversation.

questions.question: Which coworking spaces in Berlin are best for early-stage B2B startups?

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: Factory Berlin is where deals get done. The hallway conversations are worth the premium. If budget is tight, get a part-time membership and show up on Tuesdays and Thursdays when it is busiest.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: For B2B startups: Factory Berlin (Mitte and Görlitzer Park) has the strongest startup community and investor foot traffic. WeWork Kudamm is polished but corporate. Ahoy Berlin in Wedding is cheaper and more technical. Mindspace Moritzplatz is a good middle ground.

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: Also consider startup-specific offices in your industry vertical — some healthtech and fintech hubs offer dedicated spaces with curated neighbours. The serendipity of sitting next to a potential customer or partner is underrated.

questions.question: Are there good hardware-friendly maker spaces or labs in Berlin for mobility startups doing prototype testing?

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: EUREF Campus has dedicated lab and workshop space for mobility and energy hardware startups — worth applying for residency even if you are not in their accelerator program. The shared equipment and the proximity to Siemens and BMW engineers on campus is a genuine advantage.

answers.name: Jonas Reuter
answers.text: Best options for hardware prototyping in Berlin: Fab Lab Berlin in Prenzlauer Berg (open access CNC, laser cutting, electronics), Berlin Makerspace in Kreuzberg (community-run, strong mechanical engineering crowd), and the TU Berlin workshops (accessible to affiliated startups via Exist program).

answers.name: Hana Okafor
answers.text: We used Fab Lab Berlin for early prototyping. The community is helpful and the equipment is well-maintained. Book time slots in advance — the laser cutters and CNC machines are heavily booked on weekends. Weekday mornings are the sweet spot.

questions.question: We need to register a company vehicle in Berlin for our hardware prototype. What is the fastest way to do this as a GmbH?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: From a tax perspective: a GmbH company vehicle is fully deductible but triggers a 1% rule for private use by the Geschäftsführer unless you keep a detailed Fahrtenbuch (mileage log). For a prototype vehicle used purely for testing, document every trip from day one.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Register at the Kfz-Zulassungsstelle Berlin — there are locations in Tempelhof and Pankow. You need your GmbH Handelsregisterauszug, the vehicle documents, proof of insurance (eVB number), and a SEPA mandate for vehicle tax. Online appointment booking is available but slots go fast — book 2 weeks ahead.

answers.name: Tomas Berg
answers.text: We registered two vehicles for our GmbH. The Tempelhof Zulassungsstelle is faster than Pankow in our experience. Go in person rather than using a service — it is straightforward for a GmbH and you save the €150 service fee.

questions.question: What Berlin networking events bring together mobility founders, corporates like BVG or Siemens, and investors in the same room?

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: The BVG Innovation Night (quarterly, Berlin) consistently brings together BVG procurement, Siemens mobility teams, and startup founders in the same room. Also watch for the ITS Berlin events and the Urban Mobility Summit — both attract the exact mix of corporates and investors you need.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: The EUREF Campus open days are underrated for this. They happen 3–4 times a year and corporate partners like Deutsche Bahn, BMW, and Siemens send real decision-makers, not just comms people. Much better signal-to-noise than a big conference.

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: For warm introductions to BVG and Siemens specifically, the Urban Innovation Hub Berlin team can facilitate directly — they have standing relationships with both. A warm intro from them moves 10x faster than cold outreach from a conference.

questions.question: Which Berlin mobility or smart city accelerators are worth applying to for a Seed-stage startup?

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: The EUREF Campus in Schöneberg is the physical hub of Berlin mobility innovation. BMW, Siemens, and multiple mobility startups are based there. Even without an accelerator program, getting a desk at EUREF puts you in daily contact with the right corporates and co-investors.

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: Strongly recommend: Urban Innovation Hub Berlin (run in partnership with the Senate), Siemens Mobility Accelerator, and the BVG Labs innovation program. For Seed stage specifically, Urban Innovation Hub is the most relevant — they connect you directly with Berlin public infrastructure clients.

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: Also look at Techstars Berlin — they run a mobility-adjacent cohort and have strong corporate partner connections including Deutsche Bahn. The €120k investment is standard Techstars and the network access is worth the 6% equity for a Seed-stage team.

questions.question: I am building a property management SaaS targeting mid-size German landlords. In Berlin, the obvious early targets are the large Wohnungsgesellschaften like Degewo or Gewobag. Has anyone cracked enterprise sales into these organisations and can share how procurement actually works there?

questions.question: Is the Berlin Senat startup support program Projekt Zukunft worth engaging with at pre-seed?

answers.name: Erik Sandberg
answers.text: I engaged with them for a mobility pilot with BVG. The Senate connection was genuine and moved faster than expected. If you are doing anything in smart city, mobility, or urban tech, they are a real door-opener to the Berlin public sector.

answers.name: Priya Nandakumar
answers.text: Projekt Zukunft is useful primarily for networking and visibility — they run events, connect you with the Berlin Senate, and can open doors to public procurement pilots. The direct funding is modest. Worth a conversation, especially if your startup has a Berlin-city-relevance angle.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: At pure pre-seed with no product, the ROI of your time engaging with Projekt Zukunft is low. Come back to them once you have a working pilot or a live product — they will be more useful and you will have something to show.

questions.question: We are based in Neukölln and looking for a Steuerberater who understands startup equity and ESOP. Any recommendations in Berlin?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: For ESOP and VSOP structuring specifically, I recommend Acconsis Berlin or WTS Advisory — both have dedicated startup practices that understand GmbH equity mechanics, not just standard Steuerberatung. Location does not matter much as everything runs remotely anyway.

answers.name: Yara Demir
answers.text: We use a Steuerberater from Mitte even though we are in Kreuzberg — it makes no difference. What matters is startup experience. Ask specifically: have you set up a VSOP pool for a GmbH before? If they hesitate, keep looking.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Heuking and Linklaters have startup teams in Berlin that handle the legal side of ESOPs. Your Steuerberater and your Anwalt need to work together on this — make sure both understand GmbH virtual share programs before you commit.

questions.question: What is the process for applying to the IBB Gründungskredit in Berlin and how long does it take?

answers.name: Priya Nandakumar
answers.text: The IBB Gründungskredit goes through your Hausbank, not directly through IBB. You apply at your bank (Deutsche Bank, Commerzbank, Sparkasse Berlin all work), they pass it to IBB. Budget 6–10 weeks. You need a business plan, financial projections, and proof of equity contribution. IBB covers up to €500k at favourable rates.

answers.name: Tomas Berg
answers.text: We went through Sparkasse Berlin. The relationship manager matters enormously — ask for one with Firmenkunden experience, not retail. The process took us 8 weeks from first meeting to approval. Have a clean GmbH bank account and 6 months of bookkeeping ready.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: From a financial structuring perspective: the IBB loan counts as debt, not equity, so it does not dilute your cap table. Combine it with Exist or a BAFA Invest round for a non-dilutive funding stack that can carry you to a proper seed round.

questions.question: Which Berlin notary has the shortest waiting times for GmbH formation right now?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Notariat Mitte on Französische Strasse and Notar Tobias Reuter in Charlottenburg are both known for relatively fast appointments — typically within a week if you call directly rather than booking online. Avoid notaries in Prenzlauer Berg right now, waiting times are 3–4 weeks.

answers.name: Tomas Berg
answers.text: We got an appointment at Notariat Schöneberg within 5 days by calling first thing Monday morning and being flexible on time slots. Have all your documents ready in advance — the Musterprotokoll, shareholder list, and address proof — so you do not waste the slot.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Some Berlin startup lawyers have standing relationships with notaries and can get you in faster. Worth asking your Rechtsanwalt before cold-calling notaries yourself.

questions.question: How do I set up payroll for my first two employees in Germany?

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: You need to register with the Finanzamt for payroll tax (Lohnsteuer) and with the relevant Krankenkasse for social security contributions. Your Steuerberater should handle this. Budget around 20–22% employer social contributions on top of gross salary.

answers.name: Tomas Berg
answers.text: Do not forget the Berufsgenossenschaft registration — it is mandatory accident insurance and many founders miss it. Your Steuerberater should flag this but double-check.

answers.name: Hana Okafor
answers.text: We used Personio for HR and our Steuerberater handled the actual payroll runs. For two employees, Personio is overkill — a simple spreadsheet and your tax advisor is enough at this stage.

How have other AI founders managed the build-vs-optimise tradeoff here — do you fine-tune, cache aggressively, switch models, or something else?

answers.name: Nadja Becker
answers.text: This is the core infrastructure question for every AI SaaS company right now. Th

answers.name: Ben Ostrowski
answers.text: Nadja's layered approach is exactly the right framework. Adding the engineering

questions.question: We are pre-seed and got our first term sheet. What should I watch out for before signing?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: At pre-seed the term sheet should be simple. If it is longer than 5 pages, ask why. Watch out for full-ratchet anti-dilution — it is very founder-unfriendly. Also check the drag-along provisions and whether they require unanimous consent.

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: Key things to scrutinise: liquidation preferences (1x non-participating is standard, anything above that is a red flag), pro-rata rights, anti-dilution clauses, and whether the investor gets a board seat. Have a startup lawyer review it — not a general corporate lawyer.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: I have signed two term sheets. My biggest lesson: do not rush. Investors who pressure you to sign fast are a yellow flag. Take a week, talk to other founders who have worked with that investor, and get legal counsel.

questions.question: What is the fastest way to form a GmbH in Berlin as a non-German founder?

answers.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
answers.text: The fastest route is using a notary-certified Musterprotokoll (standard template) rather than a custom articles of association. This works well for up to 3 shareholders. Expect 2–4 weeks from notary appointment to entry in the Handelsregister. Use a Berlin notary that offers quick appointments — some can see you within 3 days.

answers.name: Tomas Berg
answers.text: We used a Musterprotokoll and it took us about 3 weeks end to end. The bottleneck is always the Handelsregister, not the notary. Make sure you have your €25,000 share capital ready in a business account before the notary appointment — many founders delay here.

answers.name: Lukas Brandt
answers.text: If speed is critical, some founders operate as a GbR or UG first and convert later. But for VC-backed companies, investors will want a GmbH. I would go straight to GmbH with a notary who specialises in startups — they know the shortcuts.

questions.question: Which tax advisor in Berlin is good for VC-backed startups and handles DATEV?

answers.name: Marek Sliwinski
answers.text: I recommend TaxPilot and Acconsis — both handle DATEV, payroll, and investor reporting for VC-backed startups. Pricing is typically €500–800 per month for early-stage. Avoid general Steuerberater who have no startup experience; they will slow you down at every funding round.

answers.name: Tomas Berg
answers.text: We use Awicontax. Very startup-friendly, responsive on Slack, and they handle everything from VAT filings to investor due diligence support. Clear communication and fast onboarding.

answers.name: Tomas Berg
answers.text: Also check out Founders Bay and Voldtax — both have strong startup practices in Berlin. Ask specifically whether they have handled a financing round before, and whether they can produce DATEV exports on request.
